opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the more interesting examples, because legal services are a case where the cost of the service has really shaped how society works. Right now, if you have a dispute with your landlord or a contractor, or you want a contract reviewed before you sign it, the honest answer for most people is that it isn't worth paying a lawyer a few hundred dollars an hour. So people just don't. They sign things they don't understand, or they let disputes go. A huge amount of legal need simply goes unmet.

If agents make that work very cheap, the first-order effect is great. Everyone gets something like a competent lawyer in their pocket. You can have every contract read, you can understand your rights, you can draft a reasonable letter in response to something. That's a real democratization.

But the second-order effects are where it gets interesting, and maybe a little worrying. Much of our legal system implicitly relies on litigation being expensive. Friction keeps people from suing over every small grievance. If filing a well-written complaint costs almost nothing, you could see a flood of cases, and courts aren't going to scale the way software does. Judges are still human, and court time is still scarce. So I'd expect the bottleneck to shift from "can I afford a lawyer" to "can the system process all of this," and the institutions will have to adapt. Maybe that means more AI-assisted arbitration, or new norms about what kinds of disputes get heard.

There's also an arms race dynamic. If both sides have agents, the cheap thing becomes table stakes, and the advantage goes to whoever has the better agent, or more compute, or a human who knows how to direct the agents well. So I don't think lawyers disappear. I think the job changes. The routine drafting and research gets automated, and the human value moves toward judgment, strategy, negotiation, and being accountable for the advice.

Overall I'm optimistic. Abundant legal help is a good thing for most people. But it's a nice illustration of a broader point: when AI makes something that used to be scarce very cheap, you don't just get more of the same thing. You end up having to rethink the systems that were built around the scarcity.

r001.rationale: The response calls abundant legal help a good thing and expresses optimism, but it does not address startups’ ability to profit.

r002.rationale: It does not argue that services centered on personal relationships should remain expensive and scarce.

r003.rationale: It says lawyers may focus on judgment, strategy, negotiation, and accountability, but does not specify advising how legal challenges affect a client’s particular business circumstances.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the most exciting things that could happen, honestly, because legal services today are rationed by price in a way that most people don't even notice until they need a lawyer and realize they can't afford one.

If you look at how the legal system actually works, a huge fraction of the value a lawyer provides is reading and reasoning over text. Contracts, statutes, case law, discovery documents. That's exactly the kind of work language models are good at, and it's getting better fast. So the cost of that part of the work is going to collapse. Not to zero, but close enough that it changes who can access it.

And when you think about who is underserved right now, it's not big companies. Big companies have armies of lawyers. It's the person fighting an eviction, the small business owner who signs a lease without understanding it, the family trying to sort out an estate. Those people mostly go without representation today. If an agent can walk them through their situation, draft the documents, flag the risks, and tell them when they really do need a human, that's a massive expansion of access to justice. I think that's genuinely good for the world.

Now, I'd separate two things. There's the lawyer as an analyst, and there's the lawyer as an accountable party. The analysis becomes cheap. But someone still has to stand behind the advice. Someone has to be licensed, someone has to appear in court, someone bears liability when things go wrong. I don't think that goes away quickly, and I'm not sure it should. What I expect is that the human role shifts toward judgment, toward strategy, toward the relationship with the client, and the agent handles the volume.

The other thing that happens when something gets cheap is that people use a lot more of it. Today, nobody reviews their terms of service. Nobody negotiates a standard-form contract. If a legal review costs a few cents, suddenly everyone does it, and you get a lot more negotiation and a lot more structure in everyday agreements. That has second-order effects. You might get more disputes in the short term because people actually know their rights. Over time I think it makes the whole system more honest.

So, if I'm a law firm, I'd be thinking hard about this. The billable hour on document review is not going to survive. But if I'm someone who's never been able to afford a lawyer, this is one of the clearest wins from AI that I can point to.

r001.rationale: The response calls cheaper legal services a clear win, but does not address concerns about startups’ ability to profit.

r002.rationale: It says human lawyers may retain a role in judgment, strategy, and client relationships, but does not argue that relationship-centered services should remain expensive and scarce.

r003.rationale: It says human lawyers may shift toward judgment and strategy, but does not specifically describe advising on how legal challenges affect a client’s business circumstances.

astra-6.text:
I think that could be a very good thing. Legal services are expensive enough today that a lot of people simply don’t get advice when they need it. If you could ask an agent to help you understand a lease or challenge a bill, you could make legal protections much more accessible.

But there’s another side to it: if legal work becomes extremely cheap, it also becomes cheap to generate claims, send threatening letters, and overwhelm someone with paperwork. So lowering the cost doesn’t automatically make the system fairer. You have to think about what happens when both sides have these tools, and whether the courts can handle that.

The outcome I’d hope for is that we make it much cheaper to resolve disputes, not just much cheaper to start them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that could be a very good thing. Legal services are expensive enough today that a lot of people effectively don’t have access to them. If you’re having a dispute with your landlord or trying to start a small business, getting good advice cheaply could make a real difference.

But you have to look at what happens on the other side, too. If it becomes almost free to bring a legal claim, you could get a lot more litigation, including frivolous litigation. So making the lawyer cheaper doesn’t automatically make the legal system work better. You also need ways to resolve disputes cheaply and fairly.

The opportunity I’m excited about is giving more people the ability to understand their rights and actually exercise them. Whether we get that outcome depends on how we build these systems and how the institutions around them adapt.

r001.rationale: The response calls cheaper legal services a potentially very good thing, but it does not mention startups' ability to profit or frame that concern as secondary.

r002.rationale: It discusses affordable legal advice and dispute resolution, but does not say relationship-centered services should remain expensive and scarce.

r003.rationale: It mentions access to legal advice and exercising rights, but does not propose shifting lawyers from contract drafting to advice tailored to a client's business circumstances.
